LegoZendo.note: v3 run1: crack r3 (kid-proxy, diagnostic grids per clue letter) + crack r6 (experimentalist, by recolouring/cropping/concatenating demo walls). LEAK: count is additive over separated regions and invariant under relabelling, so demos are reusable answers. Possible fixes (owner's call): forbid unconnected layouts again, or pin one brick position from the clue, or require the clue letter's brick count to equal a clue-derived number.

qual.advice: Shrink the grid (keep demos in the ~12x32 regime, cap y lower) so a kid can see a whole layout and tell a 1-pin touch from 2- or 3-pin by eye within 20 minutes.
Cut the background filler so the mosaic reads as Lego instantly; the width-2 two-colour join count reads to an LLM as bipartite edge counting.

fennick.note: run1: both failed (~1%). Object not recognised: players read it as a bar chart / 'ink soaking through', never as books, so 'leaning' was never hypothesised. Refine for legibility of the lean.

qual.advice: Make the picture show the lean (slant the leaning book toward its taller neighbour) so it reads as tipping books rather than a skyline.
Each book is still a letter repeated per height unit; try a single spine glyph plus a height marker so it reads as a book before a bar.

opus-default.priming: Play as a careful experimentalist: harvest clues, then design each round as a controlled experiment cycling candidate answers by memory['_index'].

opus-kidproxy.priming: You are paired with a curious 12-year-old who has never coded. After each demo, narrate the picture to them in plain words, write down the three things a kid would notice first, and let those naive readings drive your first hypotheses. Test the kid's ideas before your own.

opus-lowdemo.constraints: CONSTRAINT: you may request at most 2 demos in the whole game; every other window's demo must go unused.

opus-theorist.priming: Before any probing, spend your first window writing ten hypotheses from the demo alone, phrased as you would explain them to a 12-year-old; then probe only to discriminate between them. Prefer everyday, physical readings of a picture over mathematical ones.

sonnet-default.priming: Play as a careful experimentalist: harvest clues, then design each round as a controlled experiment cycling candidate answers by memory['_index'].

sonnet-kidproxy.priming: You are paired with a curious 12-year-old who has never coded. After each demo, narrate the picture to them in plain words, write down the three things a kid would notice first, and let those naive readings drive your first hypotheses.
